title: WHY DID GOD PUT ROMANTIC AND SENSUAL POETRY IN THE BIBLE?
paragraphs:
WHY DID GOD PUT ROMANTIC AND SENSUAL POETRY IN THE BIBLE?
Maybe the question isn’t why Song of Songs is so intimate. Maybe the question is why we became uncomfortable with something God was never ashamed to call good.
There is a moment when some Christians first seriously read the Song of Songs and suddenly wonder if they accidentally opened the wrong book.
The language is tender.
Physical.
Romantic.
At times startlingly intimate.
A man admires the woman he loves. A woman openly longs for the man she loves. There are kisses, fragrance, beauty, desire, embraces, gardens, fruit, longing, exclusivity, anticipation.
And all of it is sitting there...
in the Bible.
Not hidden in some forgotten appendix.
Not removed because God thought mature affection was embarrassing.
Scripture.
Which raises an uncomfortable question:
Why?
Why would the holy God put romantic and sensual poetry inside His holy Word?
Why would Scripture speak so openly about desire when desire has destroyed so many people?
And perhaps even more personally...
Why does something God created so beautifully become one of the places where human beings experience some of their deepest shame?
That is where this story becomes bigger than romance.
Because the Song of Songs does not merely confront what you believe about attraction.
It may expose what you believe about creation, sin, your body, marriage, holiness, shame...
and ultimately, God Himself.
The Bible begins with something Christians sometimes forget.
Human bodies were not Satan's invention.
God made them.
Male and female were God's idea.
Marriage was God's idea.
The mysterious union of husband and wife was God's idea.
Before pornography.
Before adultery.
Before lust.
Before exploitation.
Before heartbreak.
Before anyone used another person's body selfishly...
there was Eden.
“And they were both naked, the man and his wife, and were not ashamed.”
Genesis 2:25.
Read those final words again.
Not ashamed.
There was once a world where nakedness existed without humiliation because intimacy existed without corruption.
Then sin entered.
And almost immediately, what happens?
Adam and Eve realize they are naked.
They cover themselves.
They hide.
Genesis 3 does not teach us that the body suddenly became evil.
It teaches us that sin shattered innocence.
Humanity learned to hide.
And we have been hiding ever since.
We hide lust beneath secrecy.
We hide wounds beneath humor.
We hide loneliness beneath independence.
We hide sexual sin beneath religious appearances.
We hide marital pain behind smiling photographs.
We hide the things we searched for at 2:00 in the morning.
We hide memories.
We hide fantasies.
We hide betrayal.
We hide shame.
Sometimes we even hide from our own spouse.
Then we come to church, lift our hands, quote Scripture...
and quietly wonder whether God wants anything to do with the parts of our lives we are too ashamed to discuss.
And into that silence...
God placed a love poem.
Song of Songs does not portray biblical holiness as emotional numbness.
Listen to its language:
“שְׂמֹאלוֹ תַּחַת לְרֹאשִׁי, וִימִינוֹ תְּחַבְּקֵנִי”
Semolo taḥat leroshi, vimino teḥabbeqeni.
“His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me.”
Song of Songs 2:6.
That Hebrew verb תְּחַבְּקֵנִי (teḥabbeqeni) comes from the idea of embracing.
This is affection.
Closeness.
Embodied tenderness.
And Scripture does not apologize for it.
But immediately something remarkable happens.
Desire is given a boundary.
The woman says:
“אַל־תָּעִירוּ וְאַל־תְּעוֹרְרוּ אֶת־הָאַהֲבָה עַד שֶׁתֶּחְפָּץ”
Do not awaken or stir up love until it pleases—until its proper time.
Song of Songs 2:7.
That warning returns through the book.
Why?
Because biblical Christianity does not teach that desire is inherently dirty.
It teaches that powerful things require holy boundaries.
Fire in a fireplace can warm a home.
Fire unleashed can burn the home down.
And sexual desire is powerful.
Our culture often tells us:
“If you desire it, pursue it.”
Religious shame sometimes answers:
“If you desire it, you must be dirty.”
Scripture offers something far wiser.
Desire can be good...
and desire must have a God-given place.
That difference changes everything.
The Song celebrates desire while refusing to make desire god.
That may be exactly what our generation desperately needs.
Because we have seen what happens when sexuality becomes detached from covenant, faithfulness, dignity and self-giving love.
People become products.
Bodies become commodities.
Attention becomes currency.
Pornography teaches people to consume rather than covenant.
Hookup culture can teach people how to touch bodies without learning how to carry souls.
Adultery promises excitement and leaves wreckage behind.
Lust whispers, “I want you because of what I can take from you.”
Covenant love says, “I give myself faithfully to you.”
Those are not the same thing.
And perhaps that is one reason God allowed sensual poetry to remain inside Scripture.
Not because everything sensual is holy.
But because Satan does not deserve ownership of something God created.
Sexuality does not become sacred merely because we call it natural.
It becomes rightly ordered when it submits to the God who created us.
Biblical holiness is not hatred of the body.
It is the surrender of the whole person—including the body—to God.
That is why Paul can say:
“Glorify God in your body.”
1 Corinthians 6:20.
Think about that.
Your body can become a place where God is glorified.
Not worshiped.
Not exploited.
Not treated as meaningless.
Glorified.
And this matters because some people reading this have spent years believing their past permanently contaminated them.
Maybe you crossed boundaries.
Maybe someone crossed boundaries with you.
Maybe pornography became the secret room you kept returning to.
Maybe you committed adultery.
Maybe you were betrayed.
Maybe you confused being desired with being loved.
Maybe you handed your heart to someone who only wanted access to your body.
Maybe you keep remembering things you wish you could erase.
And now whenever Christians talk about purity, something inside you shrinks.
You hear “purity”...
and immediately remember your failure.
But hear the Gospel before shame finishes its sentence.
Jesus Christ did not come only for people with respectable sins.
He came for sinners.
Real ones.
The sexually broken.
The adulterous.
The lustful.
The ashamed.
The exploited.
The people with histories.
The people with secrets.
The people whose browser history and Sunday worship history seem to belong to two different human beings.
The Gospel does not say your sin was insignificant.
The Gospel says Christ's grace is greater.
Jesus never needed to redefine sin in order to forgive sinners.
He confronted sin...
and then did something scandalous.
He welcomed sinners to Himself.
He touched people others considered untouchable.
He restored people whose reputations had become their identities.
He carried our sins to the cross.
And there, the sinless Son of God was publicly stripped, humiliated and crucified.
The One who had nothing to hide endured our shame.
“For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God.”
1 Peter 3:18.
That is grace.
Not pretending your past never happened.
Not baptizing your desires and calling everything acceptable.
Not telling yourself that sin doesn't matter.
Grace is Jesus meeting you in the truth...
and refusing to leave you there.
Repentance says, “Jesus, what I did was sin.”
Grace says, “Come home.”
Repentance turns away.
Grace receives.
Christ forgives.
The Spirit transforms.
And slowly...
sometimes painfully...

Jesus teaches us how to love without consuming, desire without worshiping desire, repent without drowning in shame, and see another human being as someone bearing God's image rather than an object created for our gratification.
Then Song of Songs reaches one of the most extraordinary declarations about love anywhere in ancient literature:
“שִׂימֵנִי כַחוֹתָם עַל־לִבֶּךָ כַּחוֹתָם עַל־זְרוֹעֶךָ כִּי־עַזָּה כַמָּוֶת אַהֲבָה”
Simeni khaḥotam al-libbekha, kaḥotam al-zero'ekha, ki-azzah khammavet ahavah.
“Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm; for love is strong as death...”
Song of Songs 8:6.
The Hebrew word אַהֲבָה (ahavah) means love.
But listen to what the poem does with it.
Love is not described as casual.
Not disposable.
Not something to swipe through endlessly until somebody more attractive appears.
“Set me as a seal upon your heart.”
A seal speaks of belonging, identification, commitment.
This love wants permanence.
Then comes the terrifying comparison:
כִּי־עַזָּה כַמָּוֶת אַהֲבָה
Ki-azzah khammavet ahavah.
Love is strong as death.
The passage continues with imagery of blazing fire, and then:
“Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it.”
Song of Songs 8:7.
This is not cheap romance.
This is love with weight.
Love that cannot simply be purchased.
Love that refuses to be reduced to appetite.
And here Christians must interpret carefully.

Song of Songs, in its immediate literary sense, genuinely celebrates human love and desire. We do not need to pretend that every kiss, fragrance or bodily image is secretly a coded reference to Jesus.
The poetry is allowed to be what God inspired it to be.
A breathtaking celebration of covenantal human love.
But that is not where the biblical story ends.
Because marriage itself eventually becomes part of an even greater mystery.
Paul writes:
Ephesians 5:25.
Then, speaking about the one-flesh union of marriage, he says:
“This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church.”
Ephesians 5:32.
Do you see it?
Human marriage is real.
Human desire is real.
Human affection is real.
But within the wider biblical story, covenant marriage can point beyond itself.
Toward Christ.
Toward a Bridegroom whose love is not selfish.
A Bridegroom who does not exploit His Bride.
A Bridegroom who gives Himself for her.
Jesus does not stand before His Bride asking:
“What can I get from you?”
He goes to a cross saying:
“I give Myself for you.”
That is the opposite of lust.
Lust sacrifices another person for yourself.
Christlike love sacrifices yourself for another.
And suddenly the Bible's teaching about sexuality is no longer a collection of arbitrary restrictions from a God determined to ruin everyone's fun.
It becomes a revelation about what love was meant to look like.
Faithful.
Exclusive.
Patient.
Sacrificial.
Covenantal.
Holy.
Life-giving.
Which means the deepest problem with sexual sin is not merely that someone broke a religious rule.
Sexual sin takes something designed to communicate faithful self-giving and bends it toward self-gratification.
Sin takes God's gifts and turns them inward.
Grace begins teaching us how to give them back.
Maybe that is why this book makes some of us uncomfortable.
Song of Songs forces us to confront a truth we would sometimes rather avoid:
God is Lord even here.
Not just over your church attendance.
Not just over your theology.
Not just over your finances.
Not just over what songs you sing on Sunday.
Your desires belong before Him too.
Your sexuality.
Your loneliness.
Your marriage.
Your singleness.
Your attraction.
Your wounds.
Your secret temptations.
Your memories.
Your body.
All of it.
Jesus is not asking for the religious version of you.
He wants you.
The person beneath the carefully managed image.
And perhaps someone has reached this sentence carrying something nobody else knows.
You have been hiding.
You love Jesus...
but there is a battle behind the screen.
You love Jesus...
but your marriage feels cold.
You love Jesus...
but somebody else's attention has started feeling dangerously good.
You love Jesus...
but pornography keeps calling you back.
You love Jesus...
but shame from your past still follows you into worship.
You love Jesus...
but you don't know how to reconcile your desires with obedience.
Then stop pretending that hiding will heal what only light can heal.
Bring it to Christ.
Confess.
Repent.
Ask for help.
If another person has been harmed, pursue truth and appropriate accountability.
Put boundaries where boundaries are needed.
Stop feeding what is killing your intimacy with God.
And believe what Scripture actually says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
1 John 1:9.
Not some unrighteousness.
All.
That does not mean consequences magically disappear.
It means condemnation does not get the final word over the person who belongs to Christ.
The cross does.
And the resurrection proves that Jesus specializes in bringing life out of places everyone else had already declared dead.
That includes marriages.
That includes purity.
That includes dignity.
That includes wounded hearts.
That includes people who thought they had gone too far.
Maybe you cannot return to innocence.
But in Christ, you can walk forward in redemption.
There is a difference.
Innocence says, “This never happened.”
Redemption says, “It happened, but Jesus does not surrender the ending to it.”
That is the Gospel Warrior message.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Be honest.
Not to expose them. Not to embarrass them.
To remind them that God does not heal us by teaching us to hate what He created.
He heals us by restoring what sin distorted.
Sharing Christian content does not earn God's favor. Jesus cannot be bought, and salvation is entirely God's gift of grace.
But supporting Gospel work can be one practical way of helping biblical truth reach another person.
Not from guilt. Not because God needs your money.
From willing partnership.
But the greater value should never be merchandise.
It is discipleship.
It is staying close to biblical truth.
It is helping another exhausted believer encounter the Gospel again.
It is putting resources into the hands of people serious about following Jesus.
Because somewhere tonight there is a person convinced that what they have done with their body has permanently separated them from the possibility of holiness.
They need to know about Jesus.
Someone thinks desire itself makes them dirty.
They need biblical truth.
Someone thinks grace means God doesn't care about sexual sin.
They need repentance.
Someone thinks repentance means God could never want them again.
They need grace.
And somebody may discover through the Song of Songs that the God who created love is neither embarrassed by His creation nor indifferent when sin destroys it.
He redeems.
So why did God put romantic and sensual poetry in Scripture?
Perhaps, among other reasons, because He refuses to surrender love, desire, marriage and the human body to darkness.
They belonged to Him before sin touched them.
And through Christ, our whole lives—including the places where shame once screamed the loudest—can be brought under His redeeming lordship.
The goal is not merely to become less scandalous.
The goal is to become more like Jesus.
So bring Him the desire.
Bring Him the history.
Bring Him the marriage.
Bring Him the loneliness.
Bring Him the temptation.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him what you thought was too intimate, too damaged, too embarrassing or too far gone.
Bring it into the light.
Because the parts of your story you are most tempted to hide may become the very places where Christ's redeeming grace shines brightest.
Sin may have written chapters you wish you could burn—but the nail-scarred hands of Jesus are still holding the pen.
